hints: Remember that positional isomers keep the same carbon skeleton and the same functional group, only the location of that group moves along the chain.
walkthrough:
Picture what positional means**
Think of the same four carbon chain with one $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond. You are not branching the chain and you are not changing to a different functional group. You are simply sliding the double bond to a different place.

Draw the two positions**
If the double bond starts at carbon 1 you get $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. If you move it to start at carbon 2 you get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$. Both have formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$, same skeleton, different double bond position, so they are positional isomers.

hints: Focus on changing the arrangement of the carbon skeleton itself, straight chain versus branched chain, while keeping the alkene functional group.
walkthrough:
Picture what chain means**
Chain isomers differ in how the carbons are joined together. One has a straight chain of four carbons, the other has a branch so the longest chain is only three carbons long.

Choose a pair with no stereoisomerism**
A straight chain $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ has no cis-trans forms because one end of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ has two $\text{H}$ atoms. The branched isomer $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$ also has two identical groups ($\text{CH}_3$ on one carbon and $\text{H}$ on the other), so it cannot show stereoisomerism either. That pair fits perfectly.

hints: Look for the only straight chain $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ alkene that has two different groups attached to each carbon of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond.
Recall that restricted rotation about the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond locks the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups either on the same side or on opposite sides.
walkthrough:
Find the alkene that can show cis-trans**
But-1-ene $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ cannot do it because the $\text{CH}_2$ end has two $\text{H}$ atoms. 2-methylpropene $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$ cannot do it for the same reason. Only but-2-ene $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$ has $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_3$ on each $\text{C}$ of the double bond, so it is the one to draw.

Draw the locked arrangements**
Because the $\pi$ bond prevents rotation, the shape is fixed. In cis-but-2-ene (Z-but-2-ene) both $\text{CH}_3$ groups are on the same side of the double bond and both $\text{H}$ atoms are on the same side. In trans-but-2-ene (E-but-2-ene) the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups are diagonally opposite, one up and one down. Name each structure fully underneath.

Final answer: cis-but-2-ene: $\text{CH}_3$ groups on same side of $\text{C}=\text{C}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$.
trans-but-2-ene: $\text{CH}_3$ groups on opposite sides of $\text{C}=\text{C}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$.

hints: Identify molecule A from its ring drawing, it has only single bonds and no $\text{C}=\text{C}$, so think about which homologous series it belongs to.
Think about which different functional group can still give the same molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ with a chain structure instead of a ring.
Recall the classic colour change test that distinguishes a saturated ring from a molecule containing a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond.
walkthrough:
See why A and B are in different families**
Molecule A is cyclobutane, a four membered ring with all $\text{C}-\text{C}$ single bonds. It is a cycloalkane. A functional group isomer must have the same atoms $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ but a different functional group. The obvious choice is an alkene with one $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond, for example but-1-ene $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Use the unsaturation test**
You need a chemical test that only the alkene will give. Shake each with bromine, $\text{Br}_2$. The alkene undergoes electrophilic addition across the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond: $$ \text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{BrCHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3 $$

Link observation to conclusion**
With B the brown or orange or yellow colour of bromine disappears to give a colourless product. With A there is no $\text{C}=\text{C}$ to react, so the bromine colour remains. That colour difference clearly distinguishes saturated cyclobutane from unsaturated alkene.

Final answer: B is an alkene isomer of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$, e.g. $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
Add bromine (in an organic solvent) to each: brown / orange / yellow bromine decolourises to colourless with B (electrophilic addition) but stays brown / orange with A (cyclobutane, no reaction).
